title: Names That Outlive Languages
description: Britain's oldest layer: river names older than English, and hills named hill three times over

concepts.title: Fossils on the Map
concepts.contentHtml:
In 54 BCE, when Julius Caesar crossed into Britain for the second time, he wrote of a river "called Tamesis." Its descendant, the Thames, has outlived the Celtic language of the people who told him the name, the Latin he wrote it in, and the Old English of the settlers who came later. Place names behave like fossils. Words that stopped being understood long ago survive because they were attached to something that stayed put.

A farmer moving into a new valley needs to know what the river is called, not what the name means, so names pass from one language to the next as labels. Once the meaning is lost, a name can wear down or be reshaped, but it rarely vanishes. Rivers and large hills keep their names longest, since everyone in a region refers to them. Kenneth Jackson's Language and History in Early Britain (1953) mapped British (Celtic) river names across England. In the east mostly larger rivers kept them, while farther west British names survive even for small streams, tracing the slow westward spread of English.

Don't trust a modern spelling. It proves little, and guessing from it is how most place-name myths begin. Place-name scholars collect the earliest recorded forms instead, from Anglo-Saxon charters, Domesday Book (1086) and medieval tax rolls, and explain them through known sound changes. The English Place-Name Society, founded in 1923 by Allen Mawer,1 has surveyed England county by county ever since, in more than 90 volumes. Eilert Ekwall's Concise Oxford Dictionary of English Place-Names (1936) set the standard for a one-volume reference.

concepts.title: Avon Means River
concepts.contentHtml:
England has several rivers called Avon, among them the one that runs through Bristol and the one at Stratford in Warwickshire. The name is the Brittonic word for "river," reconstructed as *abona; its modern descendant, Welsh afon, still means simply "river." English-speaking newcomers apparently heard Britons call a river "the river" and took the word as its name. The same thing happened again and again, which is why the name is so common.

Other old river names carry real descriptions. The Exe, Axe, Usk and Esk share one Brittonic root, often written *isca; recent reference works tend to read it as "abounding in fish," while older books gloss it "water." Roman Exeter was Isca, the town on the Exe. Derwent, the name of rivers in Derbyshire, Cumbria, Yorkshire and elsewhere, is explained from a Brittonic word for "oak" (Welsh derw), roughly "river where oaks grow." The Thames is harder to pin down than you'd think. Its Roman form Tamesis is usually linked to a Celtic root meaning "dark," and to similar names such as the Tame, Teme and Tamar, but other derivations have been proposed, so the honest verdict is "probably, not certainly."

Even London is unsolved. Roman Londinium is clearly older than Latin, and recent work favors a Brittonic source, but no proposed meaning has won agreement. In 1998 Richard Coates proposed a pre-Celtic river name built from roots meaning "flow." The idea rests entirely on reconstructed forms with no other evidence, and it isn't generally accepted as proven. Most specialists still call the origin of the name uncertain.

concepts.title: Hill Hill Hill, and a Hill That Isn't There
concepts.contentHtml:
Because newcomers took over names without their meanings, many British places say the same thing twice in two languages, a kind of tautology. Bredon Hill in Worcestershire begins with a Brittonic word for "hill" (compare Welsh bre). English speakers added their own dun, "hill," giving the Breodun of charters dated 775 and 780; when that stopped meaning anything too, "Hill" was added. Pendle Hill in Lancashire repeats the pattern: Brittonic pen, "head, hill," plus Old English hyll, recorded as Pennul in the 13th century, plus modern "Hill." River Avon is "River River."

The most famous example is a ghost. You'll often see Torpenhow Hill in Cumbria quoted as "hill-hill-hill-hill," four words from four waves of settlers. But Torpenhow, locally pronounced roughly "truh-PEN-uh," is a village, and in 2003 the word researcher Darryl Francis, checking with local people, found no landform officially or locally called Torpenhow Hill. The trail runs back to Thomas Denton, who in 1688 described the hall and church as standing on a hill, and to Victorian writers such as G. L. Fenton, who in 1884 held the name up as an example of "quadruple redundancy."

The village name itself is still a stack. The place-name scholar A. D. Mills read it as Old English torr, "rocky peak," Celtic penn, "hill, top," and Old English hoh, "hill-spur," roughly "ridge of the hill with a rocky peak." Names do pile up in layers, though the tidy four-language joke was invented.

title: Roman Forts and English Farms
description: How castra became -chester, what -ham, -ton, -ley and -ing meant, and the people of Snot

concepts.title: From Castra to Chester
concepts.contentHtml:
Manchester, Winchester, Lancaster, Doncaster, Gloucester, Leicester and Worcester all end in one borrowed word. Latin castra, "military camp," entered Old English as ceaster, used for a Roman fort or walled town, and most places carrying it stand on Roman sites. The spelling varies with regional dialect: -chester (Winchester, Colchester, Manchester); -caster, with a hard k sound, mostly in northern and eastern England (Lancaster, Doncaster); and -cester, pronounced "-ster," as in Leicester ("Lester") and Worcester ("Wooster"). Exeter shows the word worn down even further.

The first part is often the Roman or British name of the place, reshaped. Winchester was Venta; Exeter was Isca, on the Exe; Manchester was Mamucium, a Latinized Brittonic name whose meaning is uncertain, perhaps "breast-shaped hill." Lancaster and Doncaster are the forts on the rivers Lune and Don. Chester itself, Roman Deva, was first "the fort of the legions" and then simply "the fort." Lincoln keeps a different Latin word: Lindum Colonia, a colony of retired soldiers at Lindum, from a Brittonic word for "pool" related to Welsh llyn.

Roman roads left their own mark. Latin strata, a paved road, gave Old English straet, "street," which in early names meant a Roman road. Stratford, Stretton and Streatham sit where a Roman road crossed a ford, ran past a farm or passed a homestead. So Stratford-upon-Avon decodes as "ford on the Roman road, on the river called River." Beyond words like these, Latin left few place names in England, which is often read as a sign of how sharply Roman town life broke down after Roman rule ended around 410 CE.

concepts.title: Ham, Ton, Ley and the People of -ing
concepts.contentHtml:
The Old English settlers named their own places with a small kit of repeated words. Tun first meant a fence or enclosure, then the farmstead inside it, and much later a town. As -ton it is by most counts the commonest element in English place names, giving the many Nortons, Suttons and Newtons: "north farm," "south farm," "new farm." Ham, "homestead, village," gives -ham, though scholars must check early spellings, since a similar word, hamm, meant land in a river bend or a water meadow. Leah, a wood or a clearing in one, became -ley, as in Ilkley and Otley. Burh, a fortified place, became -bury and -borough.

The ending -ing is trickier. In names like Hastings and Reading, Old English -ingas meant "the people of": Hastings was the land of the Haestingas, Haesta's people, and Reading of the Readingas, Reada's people. Combined with ham it gives -ingham, as in Birmingham, usually explained as the homestead of the Beormingas, Beorma's people.

For decades these "people" names were treated as the oldest English settlements, planted in the 5th century by bands named after their leaders. In 1966 John McNeal Dodgson compared their distribution in southeast England with pagan Anglo-Saxon cemeteries and found that the two rarely coincided. He argued that -ingas names belong to a somewhat later phase, after the first arrivals, and most scholars followed him, though some now question parts of that framework too.

concepts.title: Snot's People, and How to Decode a Name
concepts.contentHtml:
Nottingham first appears in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 868 as Snotengaham: the homestead (ham) of the people (-inga-) of a man called Snot. Domesday Book in 1086 still has Snotingeham; by the 12th century the record shows Notingeham. The loss of the S is usually put down to Norman French speakers, who found the cluster "sn" at the start of a word awkward. Nobody renamed the town. The name simply wore into a new shape, and Snot himself is known only from it.

That pattern gives a method. Find the earliest spellings, split them into known elements, and read the elements in order: the last one usually names the kind of place, and the first describes it. Oxford, recorded in the early 10th century as Oxnaforda, is "ford used by oxen." Swindon is swin plus dun, "pig hill." Bradford is "broad ford." Ashton is "ash-tree farm" and Ashley "ash-tree clearing."

The traps are real. Modern spellings mislead (nothing in Swindon's current form suggests pigs), different old words can collapse into one modern ending, and personal names hide everywhere. Reference tools help: the Key to English Place-Names, from the University of Nottingham's Institute for Name-Studies, lists meanings for thousands of names, and Victor Watts's Cambridge Dictionary of English Place-Names (2004) sets out the early spellings behind each reading. A guess that skips the early spellings is a story, not an etymology.

title: Viking Ground
description: -by, -thorpe and -thwaite, what a map of Norse names can and cannot prove, and Norse streets and brooks

concepts.title: By, Thorpe, Thwaite
concepts.contentHtml:
Plot every English place ending in -by and a shape appears: dense in Lincolnshire, Yorkshire and the East Midlands, thinning to almost nothing south and west of a line running roughly from London toward Chester. That line is close to the edge of the Danelaw, the region under Scandinavian rule after the Viking armies of the 860s and 870s, set out in a treaty between King Alfred and the Danish leader Guthrum, usually dated to the 880s. Old Norse byr meant a farmstead or village. Many -by names pair it with a Scandinavian personal name: Grimsby is Grímr's village, and a medieval legend made Grim a fisherman who founded the town. Others describe. Kirkby is "village with a church," and Derby, usually explained as "farmstead where deer are kept," seems to have replaced an earlier English name, Northworthy.

Thorp meant a secondary settlement, an outlying farm or hamlet that depended on a larger place. Scunthorpe appears in Domesday Book as Escumetorp, "Skúma's outlying farm." Norse thveit, a clearing or meadow, gives -thwaite, thick on the ground in the Lake District. Its Norwegian cousin tveit is common in southwest Norway, a hint that Cumbria's Norse settlers were largely Norwegian, many probably arriving by way of Ireland and the Isle of Man rather than from Denmark. Toft, a house plot, and beck, a stream, are Norse too.

Altogether about 1,400 places in England are thought to have Scandinavian names, most of them inside the old Danelaw. The language left ordinary words as well: even bylaw probably began as Norse "village law."

concepts.title: What the Names Prove
concepts.contentHtml:
How many Vikings actually settled? The names seem to say a great many, and scholars have argued over them for decades. In the late 1950s and 1960s the historian Peter Sawyer argued that Viking armies numbered in the hundreds, not thousands, and that a small elite could spread its names without a mass migration. The place-name scholar Kenneth Cameron replied, from the 1960s on, that the sheer density of Norse names in the East Midlands, many of them on less attractive land than nearby English villages, pointed to farmers who followed the armies and opened up new ground.

Hybrid names complicate both sides. Places like Grimston pair a Scandinavian personal name with Old English tun and are usually called "Grimston hybrids." Cameron preferred "Toton hybrids," after Toton in Nottinghamshire (Norse Tófi plus tun), because Grim is not always Norse: it can also be an English by-name of the god Woden. Hybrids may mark English villages taken over by Scandinavian lords, or simply a bilingual countryside where the two languages mixed.

Genetics added a twist. The People of the British Isles study, published in Nature in 2015, found no clear genetic signature of Danish Vikings in the old Danelaw, and its authors suggested a small Danish ruling group over a mostly English population. Jane Kershaw and Ellen Røyrvik objected in 2016, pointing to metalwork, burials and language as evidence of large-scale settlement, and noting that Danes and Anglo-Saxons came from neighboring regions and may be hard to tell apart genetically. The names prove that Norse was spoken widely. How many speakers that took is still argued.

concepts.title: Streets, Islands and Brooks
concepts.contentHtml:
In York, the Viking town of Jórvík, the streets are gates and the gates are bars. Old Norse gata, "street," survives in Micklegate ("great street"), Coppergate, Goodramgate and Walmgate, while the gateways through the city walls are called bars, as in Micklegate Bar. One of the shortest streets has the oddest name, Whip-Ma-Whop-Ma-Gate. Its origin is unknown, and the local explanations, from a whipping post to a phrase meaning "neither one thing nor the other," are guesses.

Farther north, Norse names took over almost completely. In Orkney and Shetland, which passed from Norwegian to Scottish control in 1468 and 1469, the great majority of place names are Norse. Kirkwall is Kirkjuvágr, "church bay," and Lerwick is usually explained as "muddy bay." A thin earlier Celtic layer survives, but the islands' names are among the clearest evidence of how thoroughly Norse speakers replaced what came before. Norn, the Norse language of the islands, died out between the late 18th and mid-19th centuries, yet its names remain on every map.

The same seafaring world named part of France. Normandy is the land of the Northmen, granted to the Viking leader Rollo in a settlement traditionally dated to 911, and Scandinavian elements survive in many Norman place names, most densely in the Pays de Caux and the Cotentin. Norse bekkr, "stream," became French -bec: Caudebec, recorded about 1025 as Caldebec, is "cold brook," from kaldr plus bekkr. Cumbria has the identical name, Caldbeck, coined by Norse speakers on the other side of the sea.

title: The Americas: Borrowed, Sainted, Invented
description: Indigenous words on the map, explorers who named coasts by the calendar, and a state name that may be a hoax

concepts.title: Words Borrowed from the First Namers
concepts.contentHtml:
About half of the fifty US states, 24 to 26 depending on how disputed cases such as Idaho are counted, have names taken from Indigenous languages of the Americas, and Hawaii has a Hawaiian one. Most passed through French, Spanish or English ears and arrived bent out of shape. Mississippi is a French rendering of Ojibwe misi-ziibi, "great river"; Michigan is Ojibwe mishigami, "large lake"; Connecticut comes from a Mohegan-Pequot word meaning "at the long tidal river." Massachusetts takes the name of the Massachusett people, usually glossed "at the great hill" or "by the blue hills," after the Great Blue Hill south of Boston. Oklahoma was coined from Choctaw okla, "people," and humma, "red," by the Choctaw leader Allen Wright during treaty talks just after the Civil War.

Chicago is a plant. The French explorer La Salle wrote the name as Checagou around 1679, from the Miami-Illinois word shikaakwa for a wild relative of onion and garlic, Allium tricoccum, the plant now sold as ramps. In 1687 Henri Joutel noted that the place took its name from the quantity of garlic growing in the woods.

Canada began as the word for one village. In 1535 people near present-day Quebec City used the St. Lawrence Iroquoian word kanata, "village" or "settlement," to direct Jacques Cartier to Stadacona, their town. Cartier applied it to the whole region under its chief, Donnacona, and by the 1540s European maps used it for the lands along the St. Lawrence. The popular story that Spanish or Portuguese sailors wrote acá nada, "nothing here," has no support: no Iberian map shows the name before Cartier.

concepts.title: Named by the Calendar
concepts.contentHtml:
European explorers reaching unfamiliar coasts often named them after the feast day on which they arrived. On 2 April 1513 Juan Ponce de León sighted a coast he called La Florida, because it was the Easter season, Pascua Florida, the "flowery Easter"; the green shore may have suggested the name as well. On Christmas Day 1497 Vasco da Gama, sailing along the coast of southeast Africa, named it Natal, Portuguese for Christmas, and the Brazilian city of Natal was founded on Christmas Day 1599. On Easter Sunday, 5 April 1722, the Dutch navigator Jacob Roggeveen came upon the Pacific island he called Easter Island, known to its own people as Rapa Nui.

A Portuguese expedition entered a great bay on 1 January 1502 and called it Rio de Janeiro, "January River," although the water is Guanabara Bay, not a river. Jacques Cartier named a small bay on the feast of St. Lawrence in August 1535, and the name spread to the whole gulf and river. On 13 June 1691, the feast of St. Anthony of Padua, a Spanish party reached a river and a Payaya settlement and named the place San Antonio; the Payaya called the area Yanaguana, "refreshing waters." St. Augustine in Florida is named for the saint on whose feast day, 28 August 1565, Pedro Menéndez de Avilés first sighted the coast.

These names record a date and a worldview: a coast entered Christian geography on the day a European first wrote it down. Many were laid over names already in use. Rapa Nui and Yanaguana are older than the saints' names that replaced them on European charts.

concepts.title: A Novel, a Hoax and a Misunderstanding
concepts.contentHtml:
California was named from fiction. In Las sergas de Esplandián, a Spanish chivalric romance by Garci Rodríguez de Montalvo printed around 1510, California is an island near the Earthly Paradise, ruled by Queen Calafia and inhabited by warrior women. Spaniards sent by Hernán Cortés landed near the tip of Baja California in 1533, took it for an island, and the novel's name stuck. Where Montalvo found the word is unknown; one suggestion links it to "Califerne" in the medieval Song of Roland.

Idaho may be a made-up word. It was first proposed around 1860 for the new mining territory that became Colorado, and promoted as a Shoshone term for "gem of the mountains." In early 1861 Congress heard that the name might be invented and chose Colorado instead. By then the word was in circulation, a Colorado town had already taken it (Idaho Springs), and in 1863 Congress gave it to a different territory. No Shoshone source for the "gem" meaning has been found. George M. Willing, who had posed as a delegate for the mining region, later claimed he had coined it; a less certain proposal points to a Plains Apache word.

Yucatán carries the classic "I don't understand you" story: Spaniards in 1517 asked the name of the land, and Maya speakers answered with something like "I don't understand you." The friar Toribio de Benavente Motolinía told a version in the 16th century. It may be true in outline, but the exact Maya phrase is a modern reconstruction and other explanations exist.

title: How Countries Got Their Names
description: Silver that was never there, a Venice on stilts, Spain's rabbits and a country named on paper

concepts.title: Silver, Little Venice and Red Dye
concepts.contentHtml:
Argentina is named for silver it barely had. Survivors of Juan Díaz de Solís's expedition of 1516 heard of a mountain of silver inland, the Sierra de la Plata, and Sebastian Cabot's voyage of 1526 to 1529, which collected silver objects from Guaraní peoples, helped fix the name Río de la Plata, "River of Silver," on the great estuary. The metal had come from the Andean world far to the northwest. A Venetian map of 1536 is the earliest known to use the "silvery" form for the region; the poet Martín del Barco Centenera published La Argentina in 1602, and a presidential decree fixed "República Argentina" as the official name in 1860.

Venezuela means "little Venice." The usual account says that in 1499 the expedition of Alonso de Ojeda, with Amerigo Vespucci aboard, saw houses built on stilts over the water near Lake Maracaibo and was reminded of Venice. Martín Fernández de Enciso, a lawyer and geographer who later backed Ojeda's colony on the mainland, gave a different origin in his Suma de geografía (1519): a local people who called themselves something like "Veneciuela." The Venice story is more widely accepted, but both versions come from European sources, and neither can now be checked against what the local people said.

Brazil is named for a tree. Portuguese traders shipped brazilwood, prized for its red dye, and the trade name, from brasa, "ember," pushed aside earlier official names such as Terra de Santa Cruz, "Land of the Holy Cross." A territory named for its first export is not unusual: the Gold Coast and the Ivory Coast were named the same way.

concepts.title: Spain's Rabbits, Italy's Calves
concepts.contentHtml:
Some country names are so old that their meaning is lost. The Romans called the Iberian peninsula Hispania, the source of España and Spain, but they took the name from earlier visitors, probably Phoenician traders, and its meaning is uncertain. The best-known theory reads a Phoenician i-shphan-im as "island (or coast) of hyraxes": Phoenicians, who knew the rock hyrax at home, may have taken Iberia's rabbits for them. The rabbit link has some ancient support. The poet Catullus called Celtiberia "rabbity," and Roman coins from the reign of Hadrian onward show the personified province with a rabbit at her feet. Other scholars read the same Phoenician name as "land of metals" or "northern island." The rabbit story is possible, not proven.

Italy has a similar puzzle. Ancient writers already explained Italia as "land of calves," and a link with an Oscan form, víteliú, is one modern proposal among several. Germania, the Roman name for the lands beyond the Rhine, is also of uncertain origin; Celtic sources such as a word for "neighbor" have been suggested, and a once-popular "spear" theory is now regarded as obsolete.

Folk explanations are often wrong, but occasionally an ancient story turns out to be among the scholarly favorites. The test is the same as for an English village: early forms, a plausible language of origin, and sound changes that work, not a tidy meaning. Where those run out, the right answer is "uncertain."

concepts.title: Peoples, Persons and Points of the Compass
concepts.contentHtml:
Most country names fall into a few types. Many come from a people: France from the Franks, England from the Angles (Englaland, "land of the Angles"), Russia from the Rus. Some describe the land: Montenegro is Venetian for "black mountain." Some give a direction, from someone's point of view. Austria's German name Österreich, "eastern realm," first appears as Ostarrîchi in a charter of 996. Australia comes from Latin australis, "southern," and was popularized by the navigator Matthew Flinders, who promoted it from 1804 and in his book of 1814. Japan's own name, Nihon or Nippon, means "origin of the sun," the land lying toward the sunrise from China.

Others honor individuals. America comes from Amerigo Vespucci, through Martin Waldseemüller's world map of 1507, which put the name on the southern continent. Colombia honors Columbus; Bolivia, named in 1825, honors Simón Bolívar; the Philippines take their name from Felipinas, given in 1543 by Ruy López de Villalobos to Leyte and Samar for Prince Philip, later Philip II of Spain; and Saudi Arabia, so named in 1932, carries the name of the ruling house of Saud.

Pakistan is that rare thing, a name designed on paper. In January 1933 Choudhry Rahmat Ali, a student at Cambridge, published a pamphlet, Now or Never, proposing Pakstan, built from the names of Muslim-majority homelands in the northwest: Punjab, Afghania (the North-West Frontier), Kashmir, Sindh and Baluchistan. He also pointed out that pak means "pure" in Persian and Pashto. An "i" was soon added, and the name became a country in 1947.

title: Exonyms, Renamings and Stunts
description: Why Germany has half a dozen unrelated names, how cities change names for politics, and long names built for tourists

concepts.title: One Country, Many Names
concepts.contentHtml:
The name a people uses for its own place is an endonym; a name outsiders use is an exonym. Germany has an unusually large set, because its neighbors met different Germans. Germans say Deutschland, from Old High German diutisc, "of the people," the same root as English Dutch and Italian tedesco. English uses the Roman Germania. French Allemagne, Spanish Alemania and Turkish Almanya come from the Alemanni, a confederation on the upper Rhine. Finnish Saksa and Estonian Saksamaa come from the Saxons. Polish Niemcy, Czech Německo and Hungarian Németország come from a Slavic word usually read as "mute": people who could not speak a Slavic language. Lithuanian Vokietija is of unclear origin.

Naming the foreigner is a common pattern. Wales and Welsh come from Old English wealh, from a Germanic word, probably based on the Gaulish tribe of the Volcae, that came to cover inhabitants of the Roman West; the Anglo-Saxons applied it to the Britons. Its relatives include Wallonia and Wallachia. The Welsh name for their own country, Cymru, goes back to Brittonic combrogi, "fellow countrymen." The same land is "the foreigners" in one language and "our people" in the other.

Many countries are known abroad by names their citizens do not use: Greece is Hellas to Greeks, Finland is Suomi, Hungary is Magyarország and Japan is Nihon. Exonyms are not insults by default. Most are simply old, borrowed through whichever neighbor did the naming first.

concepts.title: Renaming as Politics
concepts.contentHtml:
One city on the Bosporus has carried three main names. Greek colonists called it Byzantion. Constantine made it his new capital in 330 CE, and coins of the 330s already call it Constantinopolis, Constantinople. Istanbul is a worn-down Greek phrase, usually derived from eis tin polin, "to the City," or a colloquial form meaning "in the City." Arab and Armenian writers record it from the 10th century, long before the Ottoman conquest of 1453. The Ottomans kept Kostantiniyye as the formal name until the empire ended in 1922, and in 1930 the Turkish republic asked other countries to use Turkish names, which made Istanbul the international form.

Mumbai is a similar case. The name comes from Mumbadevi, patron goddess of the Koli fishing community, with Marathi aai, "mother." Speakers of Marathi, Gujarati and other local languages already called the city Mumbai or Mambai. The Portuguese wrote Bombaim, the English made it Bombay, and the tale that it meant "good bay" in Portuguese has no scholarly basis. In 1995, after the Shiv Sena, which called "Bombay" a colonial legacy, came to power in Maharashtra, the English name officially became Mumbai. Madras became Chennai in 1996 and Calcutta became Kolkata in 2001.

Some renamings swing back. St. Petersburg became Petrograd in 1914, because the old name sounded German during a war against Germany; Leningrad in 1924, after Lenin's death; and St. Petersburg again in 1991, after a vote by residents. In 2022 the United Nations agreed to call Turkey by its Turkish name, Türkiye.

concepts.title: The Longest Names Are Advertising
concepts.contentHtml:
The Anglesey village that signs itself Llanfairpwllgwyngyllgogerychwyrndrobwllllantysiliogogogoch has 58 characters on its station sign, or 51 letters by the Welsh alphabet, in which ll and ch each count as one. It means roughly "St. Mary's church in the hollow of the white hazel, near the fierce whirlpool and the church of St. Tysilio of the red cave." The genuine medieval name was far shorter: the township of Pwllgwyngyll, "pool of the white hazels," recorded in the 1250s. Locals usually say Llanfairpwll or Llanfair PG.

The long form was built for attention. After the railway arrived in the mid-19th century, the usual story goes, a scheme of the 1860s gave the station the longest name in Britain to draw visitors, and the Welsh scholar John Morris-Jones said a local tailor devised it. Slightly different long versions in print from 1849 and 1866 suggest it grew in stages, so the inventor and date are uncertain, but the motive is clear. The "red cave" ending seems to have been borrowed from elsewhere rather than describing anything local.

It has company. The 45-letter name of a lake in Webster, Massachusetts, and its joke translation, "you fish on your side, I'll fish on my side," are usually traced to a local newspaper editor, Laurence Daly, who reportedly admitted inventing them in the early 20th century, though a shorter version of the long name appears on a 1795 map. Colonial records give the Nipmuc name Chaubunagungamaug, variously translated, for example as "fishing place at the boundary." In Devon, the resort of Westward Ho! took its name, exclamation mark included, from Charles Kingsley's 1855 novel when developers began building it in the 1860s.
